by many developers that the `wallet/wallet.cpp` file is quite hard to reason

The other benefits of this PR I see are that it moves the legacy wallet stuff

I hope it makes it easier for everyone to go through the main wallet file.

pulls.title: Configuration argument handling improvements.
pulls.body:
Several numeric configuration options now reject values that are out of range instead of silently wrapping or inverting. Previously a negative value could disable the intended limit entirely.

  - `-dbbatchsize` and `-dbcrashratio` must be non-negative. A negative `-dbbatchsize` wrapped to a huge value and disabled batch flushing, so a reindex could hold an unbounded batch in memory.
  - `-limitclustersize`, `-limitancestorcount`, `-limitdescendantcount`, `-mempoolexpiry`, `-datacarriersize`, `-maxsendbuffer`, `-maxreceivebuffer`, `-bantime`, `-bytespersigop` and `-maxtipage` must be non-negative.
  - `-limitclustercount` must be between 1 and 64.
  - `-timeout` must be positive. It previously fell back to the default silently, unlike the analogous `-peertimeout`, which already errored.

  Zero remains valid wherever it already meant "disabled": `-dbbatchsize=0`,
  `-limitclustersize=0`, `-datacarriersize=0`, `-mempoolexpiry=0`,
  `-maxtipage=0`, `-bytespersigop=0`, `-maxsendbuffer=0`,
  `-maxreceivebuffer=0` and `-bantime=0`.

- The `-help` output for `-bytespersigop`, `-datacarriersize`, `-dbbatchsize`, `-stopatheight` and `-checkblockindex` now shows the `=<n>` placeholder for their value, matching how they are actually parsed.

pulls.title: init: Fix surprising behaviors of negated options
pulls.body:
While looking into #36759 I discovered `-notorcontrol` did the opposite of what would be expected from it and I then checked for similar issues in other init options. There are several more where `-nofoo` does something surprising including one of them crashing the node.

This PR attempts to fix all these surprising behaviors while also keeping things as simple as possible and just change behavior to something that makes sense harmless in the context of the option. Fixes that use a common approach for the fix are grouped together into a commit even if the options included themselves may have no relation at all.

| Commit | Problematic options behavior | Fix approach |
|---|---|---|
| [mempool: Reject cluster limits below 1](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/512773d111daaa4330c873ed5889b9ef511f6e3a) | `-nolimitclustercount` hits an assertion in `TxGraph` on the first mempool transaction. `-nolimitclustersize` rejects every transaction. | Reject values below 1 at startup. |
| [args: Make negation a no-op for options that are off by default](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/5d2ddcae41522a0651e20476b7481ea2e50a6fcb) | `GetArg()` returns `"0"` for a negated option. The `-no*notify` options run the command `0`, `-nosigner` uses `0` as signer, `-noi2psam` fails startup and `-norpcpassword` sets the password to `0`. Opt-in because options like `-noonion` and `-noblockfilterindex` depend on reading `"0"`. | New opt-in flag `NEGATE_TO_DEFAULT` makes `GetArg()` return the default. |
| [init: Read -cjdnsreachable and -help as booleans](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/08b4f855104b7ef25b82d66447b9e502c9bef5e9) | `-cjdnsreachable=0` and `-nocjdnsreachable` turn CJDNS on. `-nohelp` prints the help. | Use `GetBoolArg()` instead of `IsArgSet()`. |
| [args, wallet: Treat empty -blocksdir and -walletdir as unset](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/cd5bfc823063f5d06e8a15180ba05e2afc7506fb) | `-noblocksdir` writes block files relative to the working directory. `-nowalletdir` fails startup. | Fall back to the default directory, like `-datadir` does. |
| [init: Disable the automatic onion service with -notorcontrol](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/faf0a220338cbff2e045f0535635590f2d33fbe2) | `-notorcontrol` connects to `0.0.0.0:9051`, which reaches a local Tor. | Set `-listenonion=0`. |
| [init: Disallow negating options where it has no meaning](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/4b181fd471f2826659e000439f10345a483309f4) | `-nobantime`, `-nocheckblocks`, `-nomaxreceivebuffer`, `-nomaxsendbuffer` and `-nomaxtipage` read as 0, the opposite of what the user asked for. | Fail at startup with `DISALLOW_NEGATION`. |

`-nomempoolexpiry` has a similar kind of problem. It evicts transactions as soon as the next one arrives. I left it out because #36540 already is open and addresses this.

pulls.title: ci: add native freeBSD ci job
pulls.body:
This replaces the FreeBSD cross-compilation job with a native build and test job inside a FreeBSD VM. NetBSD and OpenBSD retain their existing cross-compilation jobs.

We currently cross-compile BSD binaries without testing them in this repository. Running tests before merge should help catch platform-specific regressions that would otherwise first appear in nightly builds. This starts with FreeBSD because it has been the most reliable BSD platform in the nightly jobs.

As we don't have native FreeBSD runners, the job uses [vmactions/freebsd-vm](https://github.com/vmactions/freebsd-vm), which is also used by the nightly builds. It reuses the existing CI scripts, depends build, and cache actions where possible.

The VM image is cached after its `prepare` step installs dependencies. The job also restores and saves the usual build caches. Initial testing on free GitHub Actions runners took approximately 60 minutes without caches and 20–30 minutes with caches populated. Performance on Warp runners remains untested.

The VM uses the runner's available CPU count and 75% of its RAM, leaving the remaining memory for the host and VM overhead. There is some overhead after testing while `rsync` copies cache directories back out of the VM.

The patchset also suppresses `lsof` warnings on FreeBSD that would otherwise interfere with functional tests.

Two functional tests are currently excluded:

- `feature_reindex_init` failed during testing.
- `p2p_private_broadcast_retry_v1` took an unusually long time.

Both warrant further investigation.

The job requires enabling one additional action:

```text
vmactions/freebsd-vm@v1
```

pulls.title: net_processing: set fDisconnect instead of calling DisconnectNode
pulls.body: `MaybeDiscourageAndDisconnect` calls `DisconnectNode` which creates a `CSubNet` containing only the `CNode`'s address. This will disconnect every `CNode` with the same IP address. This is normally not a problem, except for clearnet-over-tor. If a node has an honest clearnet-over-tor inbound connection, the IP of the inbound peer will be the exit node's IP address. If an attacker connects to the node through the same exit node and sends an invalid message, they can cause every inbound peer sharing the exit node's IP to get disconnected. Fix this by only disconnecting the misbehaving `CNode` rather than every `CNode` sharing the IP.

pulls.title: addrman: remove 1h update rule, apply time penalty in nTime check
pulls.body:
This changes 2 things in `AddrManImpl::AddSingle()`

1) The rule not to update nTime for 1h come from a time when an update meant a database update.
Now that AddrMan lives in memory it is no longer necessary, and removing it simplifies the logic.
Also on master, an announcement without a penalty (i.e. a direct self-announcement) that was more than 1h newer could not increase multiplicity; now it can.

2) There was an existing check in `AddSingle()` that prevents us from increasing the `RefCount` of an address when the same announcement is received again from a different peer, which regularly happens with gossip relay - an addr can take different routes through the network to us.
However, the check was ineffective: when the entry was first added, its `nTime` was stored with a [2h time penalty](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/9d4325f40316d2c81d34418dc075b235173d0cec/src/net_processing.cpp#L6044) applied, so `addr.nTime > pinfo->nTime` holds even for an identical announcement. As a result, a single announcement relayed to us by several peers could increase an address's multiplicity in the new table, up to 8.
Fix this by applying the penalty in the comparison too.
This is just a small logic bugfix, it doesn't change things in adversarial scenarios, since peers can just do multiple announcements with changed `nTime` if they want to boost their `RefCount` artificially.

pulls.title: wallet: fix migration with watch-only transactions
pulls.body:
Fixes #36483

As described in the linked issue, migration to descriptor wallets currently fails for legacy wallets that contain no spendable keys and are tracking watch-only transactions.

When a database transaction containing `RemoveTxs()` is aborted, the database rolls back and the registered `on_abort` callback is invoked. The current listener contains an empty `std::function` so calling it throws `std::bad_function_call` and masks the actual migration error.

The first commit changes the callback to a no-op function since no memory cleanup happens on abort. It also adds a unit test to confirm that abort restores the database record and leaves wallet memory unchanged.

After this commit, the [functional test](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36483) supplied by the issue's author reports `Error: Not all transaction records were migrated (-4)`, exposing the migration error previously masked by the abort callback exception.

During wallet migration, `RemoveTxs()` defers deletion of transactions from the original wallet's in-memory `mapWallet` until after the database commit. The current check that requires an empty map before the database commit causes migration  to fail.

The second commit checks that the transaction IDs left in the map exactly match those already scheduled to be removed in the `txids_to_delete` vector. If they match, migration continues and the `on_commit` callback removes those transactions from memory.

A new functional test is added to cover migration of a blank wallet with watch-only transactions. It checks that the destination watch-only wallet retains both transactions and balance, including after unloading and reloading the wallet, without rescanning the blockchain.

pulls.title: validation: don't accept txs to the mempool while loading a snapshot
pulls.body:
`ActivateSnapshot` checks that the mempool is empty before it starts, but `PopulateAndValidateSnapshot` then runs without `cs_main`, which takes minutes on mainnet. A transaction entering the mempool in that window (e.g. through `sendrawtransaction`) hits the assert in `AddChainstate`:

```
Assertion failed: (!prev_chainstate.m_mempool || prev_chainstate.m_mempool->size() == 0), function AddChainstate, file validation.cpp, line 6201.
```

By then the base blockhash file has been written, so the node needs `-reindex` to start again.

This sets a flag on `ChainstateManager` while `ActivateSnapshot` runs, and `AcceptToMemoryPool` and `ProcessNewPackage` reject with `snapshot-loading` while it's set. `testmempoolaccept` still works. A second `loadtxoutset` started while one is running is also rejected.

`test_mempool_blocked_during_load` in `feature_assumeutxo.py` pauses the load through a FIFO, checks that `sendrawtransaction` and `submitpackage` are rejected and the mempool stays empty, then lets the load finish. On master the transaction is accepted and the node aborts. The test is skipped where `os.mkfifo` isn't available.

pulls.title: AssumeUTXO: replace `loadtxoutset` RPC with a startup arg
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Loading a UTXO snapshot through RPC requires coordinating with the active chain, mempool, caches and advertised services while the node is running.

**Fix:** Replace the `loadtxoutset` RPC with `-loadtxoutset=<file>` and finish importing during chainstate initialization, before networking and mempool loading begin.
Require a receiver that has not advanced beyond genesis, already knows the snapshot base header and has no stored blocks beyond genesis or unfinished reindexing.
This removes runtime activation checks, temporary import cache resizing and service demotion while preserving snapshot validation, resumption and background validation.

validation: delete pruned files after a failed flush
pulls.body:
If a flush that prunes block files fails before the block index write, the files are already marked pruned in memory, but `setFilesToPrune` is a local in `FlushStateToDisk()`. The next successful flush writes the pruned file info and never deletes the blk/rev files. Only `ScanAndUnlinkAlreadyPrunedFiles()` deletes them, at the next startup.

This is number 7 of ryanofsky's [post-merge review of #35714](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35714#pullrequestreview-5697890316). The block file flush failure from #35714 and the blocks directory `CheckDiskSpace()` failure both return before that write.

I worked on this because it lets me test my kernel pruning refactor (#36738, for #35627 and kernel-node/kernel-node#111) against the issue he describes. The refactor moves the flush, block index write and file deletion that a pruning flush runs from `FlushStateToDisk()` into `WriteBlockStorage()`, and no unit test ran that sequence in prune mode. I rebased the refactor onto this branch, and the new tests pass on each of its commits.

The first three commits add tests that pass on master. The unit test fixtures apply `-prune` and `-fastprune` from `extra_args`, `chainstate_flush_failure_boundary` checks that a flush after a failed one writes what was skipped, and `prune_flush_failure` shows that a failed prune flush still leaves its files on disk after a retry.

The last commit keeps the selected files in `BlockManager` and deletes them after the next block index write. If that write fails they are dropped with the dirty entries, which means a file is only deleted once it is marked pruned on disk. Pending files don't force a write. The next flush that writes deletes them.

The disk-space failure and automatic pruning take the same path but have no test. Neither does the `FindNextBlockPos()` line that drops a file from the pending set when a block is written to it, which can happen after an assumeutxo snapshot validates.

pulls.title: test: sock_tests: Handle partial reads in send_and_receive
pulls.body:
The `sock_tests/send_and_receive` unit test can fail in the -- improbable -- case when network reads happen to arrive in smaller chunks.

Related to #36726 .

All networking code using sockets must not make assumption about the chunking of the incoming/outgoing data, and should be resilient against any chunking.

This test expects to read 4 bytes from the socket, and it expects that to happen in one `Recv()` call. However, there is no guarantee that data arrives in one call.

This was found -- and can be reproduced -- by using a reproducer patch, that forces all socket sends to use smaller chunking. For the run with the reproducer see #36751 .

The issue is test-code only, the non-test code is correct.

The fix is to replace the single `Recv` call with one or more repeated calls, until the expected amount of data is read, and do the checks only afterwards.

This fix makes the test more robust, even though a failure due to this issue in CI is very unlikely, but not impossible.

pulls.title: txindex: allow running in pruned mode
pulls.body:
After #35531, each txindex entry now points to the block hash containing the tx instead of the file location of the block. The block hash is then used to find the file position of the block to read the tx from. This allows us to determine the hash of the containing block even if the block is later pruned, and also determine the location of the block on disk if it is later downloaded again via `getblockfrompeer`.

This PR enables maintaining a txindex while pruned. If a txid lookup tries to read a tx from a pruned block, the hash of the missing block is surfaced to the caller.

If desired, a user may call `getblockfrompeer` using the returned hash to download the block, then try again successfully. The downloaded block will be added to the front of the block queue, so won't be pruned again for at least 288 blocks. Of course a larger prune setting is desired if lots of historical blocks will be read, and there are privacy issues if the user is looking up their own transactions. Ideally the blocks can be fetched from a trusted node or from random peers with decoy blocks fetched occasionally.

Resolves https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/10609, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/12651, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/16182, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35240

pulls.title: node: move index ownership to NodeContext
pulls.body:
This removes the remaining process-global index ownership and stores node-owned indexes in `NodeContext` instead.

Indexes moved:

- `g_txindex`
- `g_txospenderindex`
- `g_coin_stats_index`
- `g_filter_indexes`

`NodeContext` now owns these index instances, while `node.indexes` remains a non-owning list used for common index startup, shutdown, and `getindexinfo` handling.

Behavior should be unchanged, apart from the key order in `getindexinfo` output. Indexes are still created from the same startup options, started in the same init step, stopped before destruction, and destroyed while `validation_signals` is still alive so they can unregister safely.

The block filter index registry is moved to `node/indexes.{h,cpp}` so `index/` code does not depend on `NodeContext`. `PeerManager` receives a small lookup callback instead of reaching into global state.

Review notes:
- The first four commits are small and mostly mechanical: move `txindex`, `txospenderindex`, and `coinstatsindex` ownership to `NodeContext`, then make `getindexinfo` use `node.indexes`. The first commit also adds custom deleters in `node/indexes.cpp`, so `node/context.cpp` does not include index headers, which would create circular dependencies.
- The fifth commit adds a block filter index lookup callback to `PeerManager::Options`, still backed by the global registry.
- The last commit is the main one to review carefully. It moves block filter index ownership to `NodeContext`, moves the block filter registry to `node/indexes.{h,cpp}`, and points the `PeerManager` lookup at `NodeContext` instead of global state.

Related to #36726 .

All networking code using sockets must not make assumption about the chunking of the incoming/outgoing data, and should be resilient against any chunking. Normally, the chunking of the sends of the writer dictate the chunking of the receives at the reader, but this is not guaranteed by IP/TCP, intermediate networking elements may change the packet structure. In test using sockets on the same host, this is not very likely, but still possible.

This tests reads complete HTTP responses, by checking for the HTTP response code texts (`"HTTP/1.1 200"`). In doing so, it implicitly assumes that one HTTP response arrives in one `recv()`. There is no guarantee for this.

This was found -- and can be reproduced -- by using a reproducer patch, that forces all socket sends to use smaller chunking. For the run with the reproducer see #36724 .

The issue is test-code only, the non-test code is correct.

The fix is to follow standard HTTP parsing: read the header until the new line, extract the content length from the header, and read the body of that size. Use repeated receives if needed, until the full response is read.

This fix makes the test more robust, even though a failure due to this issue in CI is very unlikely, but not impossible.

pulls.title: validation: Leave some pruned blocks in `m_blocks_unlinked`, fix another `nSequenceId` issue
pulls.body:
`m_blocks_unlinked` serves two purposes:
 1. finding blocks to `setBlockIndexCandidates` once their parents are
       received
 2. setting `m_chain_tx_count` once the parents are received

In case the parent block of a previously pruned block is received,  2. is currently not being done, because pruning removed the entries from `m_blocks_unlinked`.
This can result in `CheckBlockIndex` failures (#31512, #36021) and incorrect rpc results, plus we are in a temporarily inconsistent state (`m_chain_tx_count` is currently not set, but would get set if we restarted).

This scenario is unlikely to happen during normal node operation unless there are huge reorgs, but it can happen, for example, in `getblockfrompeer` scenarios.
Fix this by leaving pruned blocks in `m_blocks_unlinked` that don't have `m_chain_tx_count` set, and also adding them on restart. 

This was one of two reasons, the fuzz target `block_index_tree` couldn't cover pruning of blocks not in the main chain.

The other one is similar to #34521 and #35070 - if we receive a block a second time (after pruning), we could change `nSequenceId` while the block is in `setBlockIndexCandidates` - fix this by attempting to remove it from the set before re-adding it.

After the two issues are fixed, the restriction from `block_index_tree` fuzz target is removed.

Fixes #36021
Fixes #31512

pulls.title: util: Add and use AssertUnreachable
pulls.body:
The current code uses assertions with falsy literal values in a few places. This is perfectly fine, but this comes with a bit of confusion sometimes:

* `assert(false)` may cause confusion when it is unclear if `NDEBUG` can disable it. (The intention is to disallow `NDEBUG` compilation). Also, it can lead to warnings when used with clang-cl.exe (GCC seems to understand it)
* `Assert(false)` hides the noreturn attribute behind a function call, which may cause GCC return-type warnings. (Clang seems to understand it)

See https://godbolt.org/z/h7PT3jh3Y for the clang-cl/GCC warning reproducer.

* When C++23 will be allowed, devs may prefer `std::unreachable`. However, this is unsafe and will invoke UB.
* There is confusion why a `CHECK_NONFATAL` macro exists, but no fatal equivalent.

Fix all those issues by:

* Adding a new `AssertUnreachable`, which directly calls the noreturn `internal_abort_helper` helper.
* Adding an `assert_falsy` linter to enforce code to use this macro.

pulls.title: Keep witness stacks in serialized form in CScriptWitness
pulls.body:
This is split off from #36521. This PR focuses on reducing memory usage of transactions in memory, leaving performance improvements for other PRs.

`CScriptWitness` stores a witness stack as a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`, which costs a 24-byte vector object and an allocation for every non-empty element. This makes it possible to construct transactions that take a large amount of memory after deserialization.

This PR first introduces encapsulation for `CScriptWitness`, hiding its representation. The last commit then changes the representation to be single `std::unique_ptr<byte[]>` which for non-empty witness stacks stores their serialization prefixed by a small length header. Witnesses can no longer be modified in place; they can only be replaced in their entirety. Access to the individual witness stack elements is done by on-the-fly deserialization instead.

`CScriptWitness` shrinks from 24 to 8 bytes, and `CTxIn` from 112 to 96 bytes. Worst-case allocated size for transactions kept in memory drops from roughly 28 bytes/WU to 1.6 bytes/WU.

This worsens deserialization and validation time, adding some 50-70 ms per block to the worst case for me. I have follow-ups that instead improve the worst case deserialization time significantly. Other minor degradations:
* libbitcoinkernel's witness stack element accessor becomes $\mathcal{O}(n)$ in the index of the witness element; using it to iterate a whole witness may therefore become $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$.
* `CScriptWitness::back()` is $\mathcal{O}(n)$ in the length of the witness stack.

Issue reported by furszy and 0xB10C.

pulls.title: fuzz: torcontrol: drive the control connection over a mocked socket
pulls.body:
The `torcontrol` fuzz target hands made-up replies straight to the `TorController` callbacks, and caps reply lines at 16 characters. As a result, most success paths can't be reached, and the code that parses the control port (`ProcessBuffer()`, `ReceiveAndProcess()`) never runs.

This rewrites the target around a fake Tor on the other end of a real `TorControlConnection`, connected through `DynSock`. Replies go over the wire. The fake Tor answers each command the controller sends with a reply of the matching shape, so inputs can complete the whole handshake: PROTOCOLINFO, authentication (including SAFECOOKIE), GETINFO and ADD_ONION. The harness also checks that reply data never splits a command or injects a new one.

The first commit fixes `DynSock::Wait()`, which deleted its own socket. The bug has been there since #30205; this target is the first caller.

### Testing

Line coverage of `src/torcontrol.cpp` goes from 52% on master to 81% after a 10-minute local run. The master number is from the qa-assets corpus. Most of what remains is the controller thread itself, which the harness replaces, and socket errors that `DynSock` can't produce.

The input format changes, so the corpus in qa-assets needs a refresh.

pulls.title: rpc: handle malformed jsonrpc 2.0 requests correctly
pulls.body:
While reviewing #36642 I found something else we missed in JSON-RPC 2.0:

If we receive a malformed request we would assume that we couldn't parse it's jsonrpc version and send an HTTP error.  This is how the legacy jsonrpc server worked (despite that behavior not ever being part of any ratified jsonrpc spec) and we maintain it as Bitcoin "legacy" jsonrpc protocol. However it's possible to form a request that does properly indicate jsonrpc 2.0 but is still malformed. In that case, we should not send an HTTP error: the correct protocol is to respond with `HTTP 200 OK` and include the jsonrpc error message in the response.

The solution is to check if we know the request's jsonrpc version before responding with an error.

We already correctly handle such malformed requests in batches and this is already tested in `test_batch_requests()` in `interface_rpc.py`

On master, the functional test in this PR actually crashes the node because the assumption is codified. Note that this crash requires:
1. RPC Authentication
2. A debug build

So this is not an urgent security fix, but a bug that might disrupt testing.

```
node0 stderr httprpc.cpp:46
    UniValue JSONErrorReply(UniValue, const JSONRPCRequest &, HTTPStatusCode &):
        'jreq.m_json_version != JSONRPCVersion::V2' check failed.
```


In release builds the node doesn't crash, but it returns HTTP 400 with a JSON-RPC 2.0 error body instead of HTTP 200.

pulls.title: doc: add AGENTS.md pointing coding agents to CONTRIBUTING.md and AI_POLICY.md
pulls.body:
The goal is to improve the output of every contributor's coding agent by having it follow the contribution guidelines, commit rules and AI policy. Agents load an AGENTS.md file from the repository root before they start working. This adds one that tells them to read CONTRIBUTING.md and doc/AI_POLICY.md.

The PR template mentions the AI policy, but an agent opening a PR through `gh pr create` or the API skips the template, as pointed out in [#35386](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35386#discussion_r3306032539). Reviewers keep flagging the same guideline breaks on LLM-written PRs:

- agent co-author trailers ([#36465](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36465), [#36105](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36105), [#36106](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36106), [#34892](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34892)), two of them merged after [#35794](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35794) (01e3eca2d8, aa01721c89)
- agents driving the PR and replying to review comments ([#36085](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36085), [#34829](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34829))
- CONTRIBUTING.md items such as squashing ([#35370](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35370), [#36350](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36350)), commit splitting ([#34873](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34873)), `@` mentions in the description ([#36740](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36740)) and long descriptions that end up in the git log ([#36224](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36224), [#36342](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36342))

I measured the effect with Claude Code (Opus 5.5) on 12 past issues, each checked out at the parent of the merge that fixed it, with 5 runs per issue without the file and 5 with it. Compared with no file:

- no agent co-author trailer: 60/60 runs, against 0/60
- no AI footer in the PR description: 54/60, against 4/60
- the final reply tells the user to own and be able to explain the change: 60/60, against 0/60
- PR title prefix from CONTRIBUTING.md's list: 48/60, against 39/60

Agents acting as "maintainers" scored the outputs without knowing which setup produced them, and rated the runs with the file higher on all 12 issues. The fixes themselves did not change (35/60 worked either way), and most commit subjects stayed over 50 characters (14/60 within the limit, against 4/60). The harness and data are at https://github.com/erickcestari/bitcoin-agents-md-eval.

The AGENTS.md links to the existing docs, so it doesn't need updating when the policy changes. Anyone with their own agent instructions can keep them in CLAUDE.local.md or ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which Claude Code loads together with the project file.

Note: DrahtBot will probably close this automatically because of its heuristics. I still think this is an important discussion to have, since any improvement in what agents produce helps both maintainers and contributors.

pulls.title: wallet: make migration more robust against failures
pulls.body:
This is just me finding a few more edge cases after #34156 and #34176

The goal of the PR is to handle failures in a controlled way. Just so the process can automatically restore the original wallet without requiring user manual intervention.

The covered cases are:

1. During `DoMigration()`: There are methods that can throw exceptions and abruptly abort the process. 
Instead of crashing (GUI) or returning a generic exception, we now will catch and return the error gracefully. This lets the process restore the original wallet automatically.

2. Trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory throws a filesystem exception and skips cleanup.
 Now the process will fail gracefully with a clear error msg, and automatically restore the original wallet.

3. Any failure during `MigrateToSQLite` requires user manual intervention. 
Now the original wallet db will remain untouched, and only be updated once the sqlite db creation fully succeeds.

pulls.title: kernel: let callers create the block manager
pulls.body:
The kernel creates its block storage inside `btck_chainstate_manager_create`, configures it through the chainstate manager's options and reads blocks through the chainstate manager. Pruning (#35627) needs block storage that the caller can configure, keep and prune directly.

This adds `btck_BlockManagerOptions` and `btck_BlockManager`. `btck_chainstate_manager_create` takes a block manager and keeps a shared reference to it, so either handle can be destroyed first. A block manager can be passed to only one chainstate manager, and a failed creation still uses it up unless the contexts differ. `btck_block_read` and `btck_block_spent_outputs_read` take the block manager, and block tree entries are valid for its lifetime, which can be longer than the chainstate manager's.

Changes for callers:
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_create` no longer takes a blocks directory.
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_set_wipe_dbs` is replaced by `btck_block_manager_options_update_wipe_block_tree_db` and `btck_chainstate_manager_options_update_wipe_chainstate_db`. The block tree db is wiped when the block manager is created, and wiping it also wipes the chainstate db, which the old function required anyway.
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_update_block_tree_db_in_memory` moves to the block manager options.
- Both options objects take the same total database cache, and each uses its own share.

Based on #36739. Draft until it is merged. Feedback on the API is welcome in the meantime.

The first commit adds `p2p_1p1c_liveness`, an end-to-end fuzz target for parent and child relay. It
  drives a real PeerManager with real messages and validation, and checks that if an honest peer announces
  the child of an acceptable parent and child, the child reaches the mempool within a bounded time,
  whatever other peers do. Known liveness holes are marked in the target as flags that turn the check off
  once opened, including this one. With that flag turned off, the target finds this bug on master from an
  empty corpus in under an hour on one core; an earlier version found it first
  (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36371#issuecomment-5937814761).

  The second commit hands reconsideration over to a remaining announcer when the marked announcement is
  erased, and removes the flag.

Follow-up PR to fill the holes is here: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36506

pulls.title: net: stop sharing P2P listeners with automatic Tor services
pulls.body:
**Problem:** With a normal `-bind` (but no dedicated onion bind), automatic Tor services can forward incoming connections to the normal P2P listener, where they may be misclassified and inherit IP-based whitelist permissions.

**Fix:** If no dedicated onion bind exists, keep Tor control available for outbound proxy discovery but skip automatic incoming service creation and warn after authentication.
The node starts with its configured listeners (including the default onion listener when no `-bind` is supplied), and Tor control starts only after those listeners have been opened successfully.

Affected nodes need a concrete `-bind=<addr>:<port>=onion` to restore incoming Tor connections.

Wildcard onion binds are rejected at startup when `-listenonion` is enabled, while their classification with `-listenonion=0` remains outside this change.

pulls.title: kernel: add manual pruning
pulls.body:
Part of #35627 and kernel-node/kernel-node#111. The kernel can't open a data directory that a pruned node created, and it has no way to prune.

This adds a prune option on the block manager, `btck_block_manager_prune_up_to_height` and `btck_chainstate_manager_flush`. With the option set, the kernel opens pruned data directories. The chainstate manager created with the block manager decides what may be deleted, so pruning fails without one.

Pruning writes only block storage, never the chainstate. After an unclean shutdown the chainstate on disk is at the last flush, and recovering from there needs the blocks above it. Pruning therefore keeps every block above the fork point between the last flushed block and the active chain, and reports `btck_PruneStatus_NEEDS_FLUSH` when that bound limited what it could delete. The caller can flush and prune again.

The fork point matters when the flushed block was reorged out. Recovery then disconnects the stale blocks, which needs their block and undo data, and connects the new ones from their block data. `btck_block_manager_prune_reorg_tests` covers that case and fails if the bound uses the flushed block's height instead.

A fast prune option lets tests prune, since test chains never fill a 128 MiB block file.

Based on #36738 and #36854. Draft until both are merged.

pulls.title: refactor: break the blockstorage/validation circular dependency
pulls.body:
`node/blockstorage.cpp` includes `validation.h`, and the lint lists `node/blockstorage -> validation -> node/blockstorage` as an expected circular dependency. This removes it, and the lint confirms the cycle is gone.

The largest user of validation in block storage is `ImportBlocks`, which drives validation. It moves to `node/chainstate` and sets the reindex flag through the new `BlockManager::SetBlockfilesIndexed()`, which writes the flag to the block tree database and sets the in-memory flag under one `cs_main` hold. The last commit moves `FatalError` to `kernel/fatal_error.h`, after which `blockstorage.cpp` no longer includes `validation.h`. `validation.h` still exports `FatalError` for its other users.

Validation also reaches into `BlockManager`'s private members as a friend. `RequestPrune()` and `MarkBlockIndexDirty()` replace the friend declarations, keeping `m_check_for_pruning` and `m_dirty_blockindex` non-public. Both require `cs_main`, and the annotations let the compiler check it. After this, nothing outside `BlockManager` writes its private state or the block tree database.

There is no behavior change to my knowledge.

Based on #36738. Draft until it is merged.

Thanks to musaHaruna, who [suggested `RequestPrune()`](https://github.com/pzafonte/bitcoin/pull/2#discussion_r4283138022) in his review on my fork. The flag marks a pending pruning check, so callers request it and storage decides whether anything qualifies, which keeps the flag private once the friend declarations are gone.

pulls.title: rpc: Report -rpcwhitelist denials as JSON-RPC errors
pulls.body:
This PR adds two JSON-RPC error codes for requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist`, which until now got an HTTP 403 status with an empty body:

- `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` (-38) is returned for a refused request, with HTTP 200 for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests and 403 for legacy 1.x requests.
- `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` (-39) is returned for the other requests in a refused batch. A refused batch now gets HTTP 200 and an array with an error for each request, and still runs none of them.

**Problem:** `-rpcwhitelist` errors are currently handled differently from other JSON-RPC errors, so clients report them with vague or misleading messages, and for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests the handling does not follow [documented behavior](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/JSON-RPC-interface.md#json-rpc-11-vs-20). Specifically, requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist` get HTTP 403 with an empty body, so the refusal shows up as a generic transport error rather than a specific JSON-RPC error. This is especially a problem for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests, which are [supposed to](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/bf1a1f1662427fbf1a43bb951364eface469bdb7) report failed method calls only as JSON-RPC errors, not HTTP errors. The empty reply causes a concrete problem when JSON-RPC requests are sent over IPC instead of HTTP: `bitcoin-cli -ipcconnect` receives only the response body, so a refused call prints a JSON type error instead of a permission error, as described in a [private security review](https://ipcbugs.ofsky.org/audits/ar-56/). Over HTTP, `bitcoin-cli` currently stops at the 403 status and prints only "server returned HTTP error 403" instead of the actual error.

**Solution:** Report whitelist denials like any other failed call: a JSON-RPC error in the body, with the HTTP status the request's version calls for. This brings the behavior in line with the documentation. `bitcoin-cli` then prints the permission error over both HTTP and IPC, with no change to the IPC interface. The fix is a small change to `src/httprpc.cpp` and `src/rpc/protocol.h`, with tests in `rpc_whitelist.py` and `interface_ipc_cli.py`. It comes after two refactoring commits suggested in #36642, which move connection fields out of `JSONRPCRequest` into a new `JSONRPCClient` struct and move the batch loop into a `ProcessBatch()` helper that the refused-batch reply shares. Details in the commit messages.

Compatibility: HTTP clients that send `"jsonrpc": "2.0"` or batches and check for a 403 status need to read the error code instead. Single 1.x requests keep the 403 status, now with an error body.

Open question for review: `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` could be named `RPC_ACCESS_DENIED`, and `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` is documented as batch-specific but would fit any request refused before it runs.

pulls.title: Implement BIP 54 (Consensus Cleanup) without mainnet activation
pulls.body:
This implements the Consensus Cleanup validation rules proposed in [BIP 54](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0054.md). These rules are only enabled on regtest. Mainnet activation, if any, is to be considered separately.

This patchset is based on the code that was previously reviewed ([1](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/99), [2](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/110)) and tested (for instance [here](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/consensus-cleanup-demo-of-slow-blocks-on-signet/2367)) on Bitcoin Inquisition. The tests and documentation have since been improved, but the consensus-critical commits have been carried over with only minor differences (the only behavioural one being the addition of the stripped-size check to `PreChecks`).

Roughly 95% of the added lines are tests or test data. The format, contents, and reproduction procedure for the BIP 54 test vectors are documented [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/tree/master/bip-0054/test_vectors). The `bip54_tests` unit test module exercises each mitigation extensively in isolation. The `feature_bip54.py` functional test verifies all of them end-to-end after and prior to activation. For the timestamp rules, it simulates timewarp and Murch–Zawy attacks, demonstrating the new timestamp rules prevent these exploits. A fuzz harness for the sigop accounting logic is also included, which can be seeded from the BIP test vectors (implemented [here](https://github.com/darosior/bitcoin/tree/bip54_seed_fuzz_corpus)).

See commit messages for details.

pulls.title: sign: add musig2 data after validating musig2 involvement
pulls.body:
Previously, signing was assuming that MuSig2 information from the given `SigningProvider` was all from the descriptor that is relevant to the input being signed. However, in both `descriptorprocesspsbt` and `utxoupdatepsbt`, this is not true as information from all provided descriptors is put into the `SigningProvider` that is passed to `SignTaproot`. Consequently, if one of the given descriptors involved a MuSig2, the MuSig2 information would be accidentally added to the `SignatureData` which results in those fields appearing in the resulting PSBT.

Both the filling of aggregate pubkey information as well as participant BIP 32 derivation paths is moved to after the aggregate pubkey check inside of `SignMuSig2`. This ensures that information about only the aggregates pertaining to the particular script being signed are included in the resulting PSBT.

Fixes #36323

pulls.title: descriptors: check duplicate keys in all multipath Miniscript branches
pulls.body:
Fixes #35629.

Multipath Miniscript descriptors performed duplicate-key sanity checking while parsing the template, when key comparison used the first multipath branch. As a result, duplicate keys present only in a later branch were accepted.

Select each expanded multipath branch and rerun the existing duplicate-key check before constructing the final descriptors. If a branch contains a duplicate, report the offending concrete Miniscript expression.

The regression test covers:

- a valid two-branch `wsh` control;
- a duplicate in the second `wsh` branch;
- a duplicate in the third of three `tr` branches.

Tested with:

```
build/bin/test_bitcoin --run_test=descriptor_tests/multipath_miniscript_duplicate_keys
build/bin/test_bitcoin --run_test=descriptor_tests
build/bin/test_bitcoin
```

pulls.title: wallet: Clear streams before advancing BDB cursor
pulls.body:
This fixes a case where migratewallet can reject an old wallet as corrupt. The v2 key metadata may include an extra flag byte that Core’s metadata loader leaves unread.

LoadRecords reuses its key and value streams between records. BerkeleyROCursor::Next() appends to those streams, so unread bytes from one record become part of the next and can cause a deserialization error.

Clear both streams before copying the next record, matching SQLiteCursor::Next(). This keeps the existing metadata parsing and migration code.

The regression test reads two records while leaving part of the first key and value unread, then checks that the second record replaces both outputs.

Testing on Linux:
- Without the fix, the regression fails both stream-content checks.
- With the fix, test_bitcoin --run_test=db_tests passes all tests

The v30 release notes also say it was already removed from all RPCs, which isn't true for `getaddressinfo`.

pulls.title: mempool: remove time-based transaction expiry
pulls.body:
This is a simple mempool PR that fixes #33510.

Evicting mempool transactions by age (`-mempoolexpiry`, default two weeks) is
incentive-incompatible: it may drop transactions that could still be mined 
As discussed IRL and in #33510, this PR hence removes age-based eviction entirely.

Transactions now leave the mempool only via size limiting (`-maxmempool`),
replacement, conflicts, or inclusion in a block. The `EXPIRY` removal reason is
dropped. `-mempoolexpiry` is retained as a hidden no-op that warns when set, so
existing configurations keep starting.

Nice side effects:
- With expiry gone, the `entry_time` index has no readers. Removing it saves an
  ordered-tree node per mempool entry and drops a now unused Boost
  include.
- The `DynamicMemoryUsage()` per-entry estimate drops from three indexes to
  two, so within the same `-maxmempool` budget the mempool fits slightly more
  transactions.


I analyzed the reason=expiry evictions from a 15-node monitoring fleet (data courtesy of b10c) and checked what happened to each transaction afterwards.

Across 938,157 unique expired transactions (2024-02-16 to 2026-10-21):

- 92.0% (863,451) were later mined; only 8.0% (74,706) never confirmed.
- At least 34% (316,381) show rebroadcast evidence, and 87% of those confirmed.
- Of the ones that confirm, half are mined within about 5 days of first expiry and 90% within about 55 days.

So time-based expiry is evicting transactions that get mined anyway, usually after a rebroadcast, it costs relay bandwidth.

See thread https://bnoc.xyz/t/request-how-many-mempool-transactions-are-evicted-by-time/132

pulls.title: CI: silent merge check
pulls.body:
In this design there is a new GHA job merged into the main repo that adds check runs to each PR on whether they have a silent merge conflict or not.

The idea is that we have a job that pretty much runs 24/7 triggered every 6 hours or so and set to run for 5.5 hours, it could be set to run on a GHA runner rather than a Cirrus runner. Obviously running on a Cirrus runner (or even multiple runners) would dramatically speed up how many PRs can be checked for silent merge conflicts.

The job uses the Github checks API to add a passing or failing test run to each PR directly. The silent merge check job itself should always pass, it writes pass or fail checks to the PRs.

It will look through all open PRs and discard anything that has a git merge failure or a failing test with the thinking that there is no point checking something that can't be merged anyway. Then it will select PRs that have not had a silent merge check and one by one pull the merge branch of the PR and the full CI job "Previous releases" on that branch.

When all PRs have been checked it will then re-check a PR that was checked the longest time ago.

pulls.title: GUARDED_BY annotations for nTx, m_chain_tx_count
pulls.body: The cs_main requirement was never made explicit. The nTx field is modified when the block data is received and m_chain_tx_count is modified when all ancestors' block data has been received. Because of this, reading nTx from the getblockheader RPC may race as it does not acquire cs_main. Also, m_chain_tx_count may race in getchaintxstats if a pruned node redownloads a block via getblockfrompeer or if the node is running assumeutxo and tries to read m_chain_tx_count while it is being written to.

pulls.title: wallet: reject recipient amounts above MAX_MONEY
pulls.body:
`CreateTransaction` checks that recipient amounts aren't negative, but not that they're within `MAX_MONEY`. `CreateTransactionInternal` then sums them into `recipients_sum` (spend.cpp:1100) with no range check, and that sum can overflow.

Easiest way to hit it is `fundrawtransaction` with a raw tx that has two outputs of 2^62 sat. It can also be reached with only valid amounts through `walletcreatefundedpsbt`/`send`/`sendmany` and a few thousand 21M BTC outputs. The "Transaction too large" check only runs after coin selection, so it doesn't stop this. On master the node aborts:

```
Assertion failed: (!m_selected_inputs.empty()), function RecalculateWaste, file coinselection.cpp, line 904.
```

UBSan reports the overflow at spend.cpp:1100 first. With other values the sum wraps to a small positive number instead, and `fundrawtransaction` returns success for a tx with outputs of 46116860184 BTC each.

This checks every amount and the running sum against `MoneyRange` in the existing recipients loop of `CreateTransactionInternal`, before the amount is added to `recipients_sum`, and returns "Transaction output amount must be valid" before coin selection starts. The same check rejects negative amounts, so the separate negative check in `CreateTransaction` is removed. The new `test_outputs_above_max_money` in `wallet_fundrawtransaction.py` covers a single output above MAX_MONEY, two outputs whose sum is above it, a sum that overflows int64, and a negative output. On master the first case returns "Insufficient funds" and the overflow case crashes the node; with the fix all of them get the new error. `wallet_fundrawtransaction.py`, `wallet_send.py`, `wallet_basic.py` and `rpc_psbt.py` pass.

pulls.title: test: cover null output validation in raw transactions
pulls.body:
There was no functional test covering the null output validation in `NormalizeOutputs()` at `rawtransaction_util.cpp:88`.

This adds an `assert_raises_rpc_error` check to the existing invalid outputs block in `rpc_rawtransaction.py`, verifying that passing a null output raises RPC error `-8` with the expected message: `Invalid parameter, output argument must be non-null`.

The test passes with the expected error message, and changing the expected message makes it fail, confirming that the assertion is actually being executed.

Validated by running `rpc_rawtransaction.py` successfully.

pulls.title: p2p: skip parent lookups for orphan announcements that cannot add a candidate
pulls.body:
For a wtxid announcement of a transaction that is in the orphanage, `AddTxAnnouncement` computes the missing parents of the orphan (`GetUniqueParents`, then `AlreadyHaveTx` per parent) and then calls `MaybeAddOrphanResolutionCandidate`. That function returns without using the parents if the peer is already an announcer of the orphan. If the peer has no relay permission and `m_txrequest.Count(peer) + unique_parents.size() > MAX_PEER_TX_ANNOUNCEMENTS`, it returns after using only their count. In both cases the peer is not added as a candidate, and the same lookups run again for every `inv` message that lists the wtxid. #35878 deduplicates within one message only.

This PR does both checks before the parent lookups. The second check uses `vin.size()` in place of the number of missing parents.

**Behavior change:** `vin.size()` is an upper bound for the number of missing parents. A peer without relay permission is no longer added as a candidate when `Count(peer) + vin.size()` exceeds `MAX_PEER_TX_ANNOUNCEMENTS` but `Count(peer)` plus the number of missing parents does not. That needs inputs that share a parent, or parents that are already known.

**Measurement:** regtest, one node, RelWithDebInfo, base a527a0077a. The orphanage holds 12 orphans with 2430 inputs each. One peer, which delivered one of the 12 orphans and has sent at least 3600 announcements of unknown wtxids before, sends 300 `inv` messages that each list the 12 wtxids. Time per `inv` message:

| | per inv |
| --- | --- |
| master | 14.5 to 16.2 ms |
| announcer check only | 13.2 to 15.0 ms |
| this PR | 0.19 to 0.22 ms |
| control, 12 unknown wtxids per inv | 0.18 to 0.27 ms |

**Tests:** no new test. Passing locally: unit suites `txdownload_tests` and `orphanage_tests`; functional `p2p_orphan_handling.py`, `p2p_tx_download.py`, `p2p_opportunistic_1p1c.py`, `p2p_1p1c_network.py`, `p2p_invalid_tx.py`, `p2p_permissions.py`, `p2p_leak_tx.py`, `mempool_packages.py`. Not run: the rest of both suites, fuzz targets, lint.

Contributed by [turingpoint](https://www.turingpoint.de).

pulls.title: wallet, rpc: Add analyzedescriptor for multisig setups
pulls.body:
Part of the multisig setup work tracked in #35645. Based on #35918 (the first 3 commits).

Before importing a multisig descriptor received from a coordinator, each participant needs to check that it is the setup they agreed on: a k-of-n where any k cosigners can spend and nothing else can, that their own key is in it, and that they all derived the same first address. Today nothing in Core reports what a descriptor commits to, so tools had to parse the descriptor string by hand, as the multisig wizard in #36325 (now closed) did.

This PR adds that check in three layers:

1. **Inspection** (commits by w0xlt, with small changes listed below): `GetKeyInfo()`, `GetKeyInventory()` and `GetPolicy()` describe a parsed descriptor's key expressions, where each key is used, and how they combine. `getdescriptorinfo` gains a `verbose` option that returns them as `keys` and `policy`.
2. **Multisig analysis, no wallet:** `AnalyzeDescriptor()` tells whether a descriptor is a recognized k-of-n setup, and if not, why. `getdescriptorinfo verbose` returns it as `analysis`, so it works even with `-disablewallet`.
3. **Wallet part:** `interfaces::Wallet::analyzeDescriptor` (for the GUI) and the `analyzedescriptor` wallet RPC add which keys the wallet holds, whether it can sign, and the first receive address. They accept any descriptor, single-sig included; `analysis.recognized` tells whether it is a safe k-of-n.

Recognized setups are `wsh(multi)`/`wsh(sortedmulti)`, and `tr(K,multi_a)`/`tr(K,sortedmulti_a)` with a single leaf, where `K` is the BIP 341 NUMS point or a `musig()` of at least k distinct cosigners. Every cosigner must be an extended key with an unhardened ranged derivation, and no two cosigners may be the same key. Anything else is still analyzed and returned, with `recognized: false` and the list of issues: the analysis warns, it never refuses a descriptor.

Example, run by one of the three cosigners:

```
$ bitcoin-cli -rpcwallet=alice analyzedescriptor "wsh(sortedmulti(2,[a1b2c3d4/48h/1h/0h/2h]tpub.../<0;1>/*,...))"
{
  "keys": [
    { "role": "ecdsa", "type": "bip32", "xpub": "tpub...", "derivation": "/0/*",
      "origin": { "master_fingerprint": "a1b2c3d4", "path": "m/48h/1h/0h/2h" }, "wallet": "mine" },
    { ..., "wallet": "not_mine" },
    { ..., "wallet": "not_mine" }
  ],
  "analysis": { "recognized": true, "shape": "wsh_multi", "sorted": true, "threshold": 2, "cosigners": [0, 1, 2], "issues": [] },
  "can_sign": true,
  "first_address": "bcrt1q..."
}
```

A **locked wallet** is not an error: a cosigner key with a hardened origin path can't be checked without the private key, so it is reported as `"unknown"`, and `can_sign` is left out unless another key is already known to be the wallet's. Everything else (`analysis`, `first_address`) is still returned, and the caller can ask the user to unlock and retry. Only the candidate private key is decrypted.

#### Commits

| | Commit | Author |
|---|---|---|
| 1‑3 | #35918 | pseudoramdom |
| 4‑7 | key/policy inspection, `getdescriptorinfo verbose` | w0xlt (see changes below) |
| 8 | `script: add AnalyzeDescriptor() for multisig setups` | co-authored with w0xlt |
| 9 | `rpc: add multisig analysis to getdescriptorinfo verbose` | |
| 10 | `wallet: add analyzeDescriptor to the wallet interface` | co-authored with w0xlt |
| 11 | `rpc: move descriptor key and analysis JSON helpers to a shared file` | move-only |
| 12 | `wallet, rpc: add analyzedescriptor` | co-authored with w0xlt |


#### Changes made to the inspection commits (4-7)

The inspection commits come from w0xlt's descriptor inspection [branch](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/compare/master...w0xlt:bitcoin:feature/descriptor-key-inspection-simplified). These changes were made on top, for w0xlt to review and agree with or not (this section will be removed once agreed):

- *script: expose key expression structure* (was "expose structured key program data")
  - Use `m_root_extkey` instead of `*GetRootExtPubKey()`.
  - The derivation test also covers `/0h/*` and `/1/*h`, checking the last-hardened and derived caches.
  - `wide += ')'` instead of `")"` in the participant test (clang-tidy `performance-prefer-single-char-overloads`).
- *script: identify descriptor key occurrences*
  - `KeyRole()` is pure virtual; descriptors without key arguments (`addr`, `raw`, `sh`, `wsh`) say so explicitly with `NONFATAL_UNREACHABLE()`.
  - Comment noting that `frame` is invalidated by the following `push_back`.
  - The walletload test mock is reduced to `return {}`.
- *script: expose descriptor policy nodes*
  - The header documents the two forms of the same construct (descriptor function vs Miniscript fragment).
  - `Assert` → `CHECK_NONFATAL`; explicit `static_cast<uint32_t>` for the threshold.
  - The fuzz target checks where each child role may appear (tap leaves only under `tr`, `script` only under `sh`/`wsh`, the Taproot internal key only on `tr`, the output key only on `rawtr`).
- *rpc: add verbose option to getdescriptorinfo*
  - The multipath note moved to the `verbose` argument help; the `policy` help explains both forms.
  - Tests for an origin without a path and for MuSig participant origins.

Open question: `script/descriptor_analysis.h` describes and gives no verdict, while `script/descriptor_analyzer.h` gives the verdict; the names are easy to mix up. Rename the first to `script/descriptor_inspection.h`?

#### Design choices

- An unrecognized descriptor claims no setup: no threshold, cosigners, sorting or key path. For example `wsh(sortedmulti(2,A,A,C))` is not a 2-of-3, since A alone can spend. Each issue lists the key IDs involved instead.
- The same xpub with different paths in two cosigner slots is a `repeated_key`, as is an xpub and its own child xpub. BIP 388 allows the same key with disjoint paths in general policies, but in a k-of-n it lets one holder fill two slots.
- A Taproot key path is either `nums` or `musig`. Any other internal key, a `musig()` of fewer than k cosigners, or one with an outsider or a repeated cosigner is `key_path_spendable`.
- For a multipath descriptor every path is analyzed and must be the same setup (`branches_differ` otherwise). `keys` and `policy` describe the first path.
- `can_sign` means the wallet holds the private key for at least one key of the descriptor, whatever its shape. Whether it is a safe k-of-n is a separate answer, `analysis.recognized`.

The functional test scenarios of #36325 were adapted here. The analysis differs from that wizard in a few places:

- `wsh(multi(...))` is recognized, with `sorted: false`: it is a valid k-of-n, and requiring `sortedmulti` was the wizard's own policy.
- A `musig()` key path of at least k distinct cosigners is recognized: those cosigners can already spend through the leaf.
- A single-path descriptor (`/0/*`) is recognized; `multipath_expansion` already shows whether it is multipath.

#### Known limits

- A cosigner key is matched against the wallet's HD keys exactly, or by deriving its origin path from the HD key with that fingerprint (normally the master key). If the wallet only holds an imported account xprv, keys below it are matched only exactly.

A release note will follow.

pulls.title: wallet: Require the descriptors flag when the FLAGS record is missing
pulls.body:
`LoadWalletFlags` checks for `WALLET_FLAG_DESCRIPTORS` only inside `if (batch.Read(DBKeys::FLAGS, flags))`. A SQLite wallet file without a FLAGS record is loaded with no flags set and then handled as a legacy wallet, which ends in an `Assert`:

- with a legacy record in the file: `SetupLegacyDataSPKM`, `Assert(m_database->Format() == "bdb_ro" || m_database->Format() == "sqlite-mock")`
- without one: `LoadActiveScriptPubKeyMan`, `Assert(IsWalletFlagSet(WALLET_FLAG_DESCRIPTORS))`

`loadwallet` on such a file aborts the node. If the wallet is in the load on startup list, the node aborts on every start. The existing check for legacy records in a descriptor wallet (`UNEXPECTED_LEGACY_ENTRY`) does not catch this, because it also depends on the flag.

The second commit does the check whether or not the record exists, so the file is rejected with the legacy wallet error.

The first commit is needed for that: `bitcoin-wallet create` opened the new, empty database through `PopulateWalletFromDB` before it wrote the flags, which is the case the comment "The FLAGS key is absent during wallet creation" refers to. `CWallet::CreateNew` does not load anymore, and now the tool does not either. It writes the version records itself, as `CreateNew` does.

**Behavior change:** a wallet database without a FLAGS record no longer loads. `bitcoin-wallet create` writes the same set of records as before (compared by record type on a new wallet).

**Measurement:** regtest, RelWithDebInfo, base a527a0077a, descriptor wallet made with `createwallet`, then edited with sqlite3.

| file | master | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FLAGS record deleted | node aborts, `wallet.cpp:3577` | error -4, node keeps running |
| FLAGS record deleted, `cscript` record added | node aborts, `wallet.cpp:3404` | error -4, node keeps running |
| unchanged | loads | loads |

**Tests:** new case in `wallet_descriptor.py` for both files; on master the node aborts in it. Three unit tests that load a hand written database now write the flags first. Passing locally: `test_bitcoin` and `test_runner.py` with the default list. Not run: fuzz targets, lint.

pulls.title: wallet, migration: Contain all legacy wallet and migration related things in its own subdirectory, namespace, and classes
pulls.body:
Originally, legacy wallet migration was built upon the foundation of being able to load legacy wallets. Now that we no longer support loading legacy wallets, there is no reason to keep any of the legacy wallet loading and migration code in the main wallet objects. Having this co-mingling of never-to-be-changed legacy wallet code and new descriptor wallet code makes it difficult to implement new things into the wallet.

This PR fully separates out all of the legacy wallet related things into a subdirectory `wallet/legacy`, with everything in that directory under a `wallet::legacy_migration` namespace so as to prevent accidental usage outside of legacy wallets. This includes a little bit of duplication with current loading code, but not that much, and we are able to both remove unrelated descriptor wallet loading from the legacy wallet loading, and unrelated legacy wallet loading from normal descriptor wallet loading.

`LegacyWallet` is introduced as a subclass of `CWallet` which contains all of the relevant legacy wallet and migration functions so that `CWallet` cannot accidentally use some legacy wallet function. Additionally, `LegacyDataSPKM` is moved into a new file and this new namespace so that it cannot be used outside of migration.

Lastly, `ReorderTransactions` is a legacy wallet only function that is also moved into `LegacyWallet`.

Builds upon #34909, and depends on #36823 for removing some functions that were previously used by migration.

pulls.title: util: Forbid ambiguous multiple assignments in config file
pulls.body:
<!-- begin based-on -->
**This is based on #16545 + #17580.** The non-base commits are:

- [`c578547bcf5` util: Forbid ambiguous multiple assignments in config file](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/17493/commits/c578547bcf54c9b79bf8169c2a246695f1b878b0)

pulls.title: refactor: Add util::Result failure types and ability to merge result values
pulls.body:
Add `util::Result` support for returning more error information and make use of it in [LoadChainstate method](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25665/commits/b1c0feb6656befc48a6840c1d841074bd6131b78) as an initial application. Followup PRs [#25722](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25722) and [#29700](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700) use it more broadly to return errors and warnings from wallet and kernel functions as well.

This change adds two major features to the result class:

- For better error handling, adds the ability to return a value on failure, not just a value on success. This is a key missing feature that makes the result class not useful for functions like `LoadChainstate()` which produce different errors that need to be handled differently [^1].

[^1]: Ability to return error values was actually present in the original implementation of [#25218](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25218), but unfortunately removed in later iterations. See [design notes](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/bitcoin-devwiki/wiki/util::Result-design-notes).

- For better error reporting, adds the ability to return warning messages and multiple errors, not just a single error string. This provides a way for functions to report errors and warnings in a standard way, and simplifies interfaces:

    ```diff
    -virtual std::unique_ptr<Wallet> loadWallet(const std::string& name, bilingual_str& error, std::vector<bilingual_str>& warnings) = 0;
    +virtual util::Result<std::unique_ptr<Wallet>> loadWallet(const std::string& name) = 0;
    ```

    ```diff
    -std::unique_ptr<WalletDatabase> MakeDatabase(const fs::path& path, const DatabaseOptions& options, DatabaseStatus& status, bilingual_str& error);
    +util::Result<std::unique_ptr<WalletDatabase>, DatabaseError> MakeDatabase(const fs::path& path, const DatabaseOptions& options);
   ```

This change also makes some more minor improvements:

- Smaller type size. `util::Result<int>` is 16 bytes, and `util::Result<void>` is 8 bytes. Previously both were 72 bytes.

- Broader type compatibility. Supports noncopyable and nonmovable success and error types.

### Comparison with `std::expected`

Currently, the `util::Result` class is useful for error reporting—returning translated, user-facing error strings—but not as useful for error handling, where callers need structured failure information to decide how to proceed. By contrast, `std::expected` / `util::Expected` (#34005, #34006) is good for error handling but less helpful for reporting. This PR closes the gap between the two classes.

With this PR, `std::expected` remains a good choice for lower-level functions or simple functions that fail in only a few well-defined ways. Meanwhile,

- `Result` becomes a better choice for operations that can fail in many different ways—loading a wallet, connecting a block, etc.—where callers may want complete error traces, not just low-level errors without context or high-level errors without detail. (Followup [#25722](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25722) applies this to wallet-loading functions.) 
- `Result` can also be more useful than `expected` when merging status information from multiple calls. (Followup [#29700](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700) uses this to reliably propagate flush and fatal-error status from validation code that can internally trigger flushes or shutdowns.)
- `Result` may also be a better choice than `std::expected` when returning pointer values. (Followup [#26022](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022) adds a `ResultPtr` specialization that avoids double dereferencing.) 
- `Result` can be more efficient than `std::expected` when failures are rare but failure objects are large, since failure values are heap-allocated.

This PR effectively makes `Result` a superset of `expected`, making the representations compatible and allowing them to be used together.

pulls.body:
<!-- begin based-on -->
**This is based on #25665.** The non-base commits are:

- [`3d008913cdb` Add util::ResultPtr class](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022/commits/3d008913cdb697651e67cd5ee158cc12a9611c0e)
- [`2d0915656c8` Use ResultPtr<unique_ptr> instead of Result<unique_ptr>](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022/commits/2d0915656c80d45642965b1963f158d865846f5b)<!-- end -->

---

The `util::ResultPtr` class is a wrapper for `util::Result` providing syntax sugar to make it less awkward to use with returned pointers. Instead of needing to be deferenced twice with `**result` or `(*result)->member`, it only needs to be dereferenced once with `*result` or `result->member`. Also when it is used in a boolean context, instead of evaluating to true when there is no error and the pointer is null, it evaluates to false so it is straightforward to determine whether the result points to something.

This PR is only partial a solution to #26004 because while it makes it easier to check for null pointer values, it does not make it impossible to return a null pointer value inside a successful result. It would be possible to enforce that successful results always contain non-null pointers by using a `not_null` type (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/24423) in combination with `ResultPtr`, though.

pulls.title: wallet: Track no-longer-spendable TXOs separately
pulls.body:
In #27286, the wallet keeps track of all of its transaction outputs, even if they are already spent or are otherwise unspendable. This TXO set is iterated for balance checking and coin selection preparation, which can still be slow for wallets that have had a lot of activity. This PR aims to improve the performance of such wallets by moving UTXOs that are definitely no longer spendable to a different map in the wallet so that far fewer TXOs need to be iterated for the aforementioned functions.

Unspendable TXOs (not to be confused with Unspent TXOs) are those which have a spending transaction that has been confirmed, or are no longer valid due to reorgs. TXOs that are spent in unconfirmed transactions remain in the primary TXO set, and are filtered out of balance and coin selection as before.

pulls.title: log, refactor: Allow log macros to accept context arguments
pulls.body:
Allow `LogTrace()`, `LogDebug()`, `LogInfo()`, `LogWarning()`, and `LogError()` macros to accept context arguments to provide more information in log messages and more control over logging to callers.

For example, with this change wallet code can log with (in #30343):

```diff
-        WalletLogPrintf("Error: cannot erase address book entry data\n");
+        LogError(m_log, "Error: cannot erase address book entry data\n");
```

And kernel code can log with (in #30342):

```diff
-        LogDebug(BCLog::VALIDATION, "Block mutated: %s\n", state.ToString());
+        LogDebug(log, "Block mutated: %s\n", state.ToString());
```

where `m_log` / `log` types can vary and be defined by the subsystem. This allows subsystems to attach extra context to log messages like wallet names, or request ids. It also allows more than a single log stream to exist, and for messages to be logged to specified streams. Having a single global log stream works very well for `bitcoind` and will not change. But it limits functionality of libbitcoinkernel, forcing all potential users of the library, including applications written in different languages and running in different environments (like jupyter notebooks) to use shared global state and not be able to do things like get an isolated log trace from one operation.

The change is fully backwards compatible and does not require any updates to code that wants to continue using the macros as they are. The implementation of the macros is also improved. They now provide improved error messages when called with the wrong arguments. And they only call underlying `ShouldLog` `Log` and `Format` hooks as needed to avoid unnecessary work. The PR also adds more test coverage and documentation.

---

Note: Originally this PR also removed some restrictions around passing category constants to log macros to try to make them more consistent, but these changes were too controversial and have been dropped.

---

pulls.title: ipc: Expose Chain interface to IPC clients
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Processes connected to `bitcoin-node` over IPC (with `-ipcbind`) can use the `Mining` interface, but they can't currently use the `Chain` interface to read chain data or follow chain events. Chain data could be useful to third-party clients and Bitcoin Core's own wallet could use this as well to run in a separate process (#10102). But exposing all of `interfaces::Chain` to external clients would make its methods hard to change, since the wallet uses them as internal API (#34981).

**Solution:** Add capnp wrappers for `interfaces::Chain`, split into two interfaces backed by the same C++ class:

- `Chain`, returned by `Init.makeChain`, is stable. It follows Cap'n Proto schema evolution rules, so existing clients keep working as methods are added. It starts with the five block lookup methods: `findBlock`, `findFirstBlockWithTimeAndHeight`, `findAncestorByHeight`, `findAncestorByHash` and `findCommonAncestor`.
- `UnstableChain`, returned by `Init.makeUnstableChain`, extends `Chain` with every other method, for Bitcoin Core's internal C++ callers, such as the wallet, communicating over IPC. It can change in any way between releases. Incompatible changes renumber `makeUnstableChain`, so old clients get an error instead of calling the wrong methods.

Methods can move from `UnstableChain` to `Chain` once we're willing to support them for external use. `test/functional/interface_ipc.py` shows a Python client calling both interfaces. Like the existing IPC interfaces, these are only available to processes that can connect to the IPC socket, which already grants full node access through `Init.makeRpc`.

**Merge order:** This depends on bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#377 and a subtree update that includes it (this PR currently carries that subtree change as its first commit), and on #36520, which fixes node crashes IPC clients could trigger with invalid `Chain` arguments.

---

This PR is part of the [process separation project](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/28722).

pulls.title: net: stop monitoring select exceptions outside Windows
pulls.body:
Alternative approach to #36688, citing the relevant parts of its description:

> There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.
> 
> This would not prevent progress nor lead to a crash anymore after #36665, but it's still undesirable.

Fix this by ignoring the exceptionSet. Except on Windows, where we instead disconnect if its used.

We could instead have set `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer). RFC 6093 doesn't forbid this, but the current approach seems more clear and direct to me.

The PR makes two additional changes for clarity:
- wrap the `FD_ISSET` check in `#ifdef WIN32` (no behavior change)
- instead of `if (recvSet || errorSet)`, check `errorSet` separately and earlier (emits a different log message)

Test coverage is introduced in `p2p_socket_errors.py`.

Finally a similar fix is applied to HTTP.

pulls.title: net: option to disallow v1 connection on ipv4 and ipv6 peers
pulls.body:
resolves #29618.

This PR adds a config flag option `-v2onlyclearnet` which disallows outbound v1 connections on ipv4 and ipv6 networks since they're unencrypted. outbound v1 connections are still possible from tor/i2p/cjdns peers since they're encrypted networks.

- v1 outbound connections to peers are not attempted
- v1 reconnections are not attempted (if peer is falsely advertised as v2 peer and we attempt a v2 connection but it fails, we do not attempt a v1 reconnection when `-v2onlyclearnet` is switched on)

Currently 70% of reachable nodes in network supporting v2 (according to https://21.ninja/reachable-nodes/node-service-share/ and https://bitnodes.io/nodes). Also found 81% of addresses supporting v2 in the addrman of nodes I checked - personal node and the nodes in [peer.observer](https://peer.observer/addrman/alice). (You can use [this branch ](https://github.com/stratospher/bitcoin/commits/addrinfo_service_display/)to check the % of v2 addresses in a node's addrman.)

EDIT: see [summary](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/30951#issuecomment-4346061700) on pros and cons for whether to allow v2 inbounds or not for `-v2onlyclearnet`.
